Medicine-04.question: ১) What is the main difference in composition between the plasma and interstitial fluid?
২) Sodium mainly reabsorbed in the..
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is proximal renal tubule (PCT). The majority of filtered sodium (~65–70%) is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.

Key points:

  • Na⁺ reabsorption in PCT occurs along with:

    • Water

    • Glucose

    • Amino acids

    • Bicarbonate

  • Driven mainly by the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump on the basolateral membrane

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Loop of Henle → Reabsorbs about 20–25% sodium, mainly in the thick ascending limb.

  • Early distal tubule → Reabsorbs about 5% sodium via Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter.

  • Late distal tubule → Small amount of sodium reabsorption regulated by aldosterone.

High-yield sodium reabsorption:

Site Approximate Na⁺ reabsorption
Proximal tubule 65–70%
Thick ascending limb 20–25%
Early distal tubule ~5%
Collecting duct <5% (aldosterone regulated)

Exam pearl:
Maximum sodium reabsorption occurs in the proximal renal tubule.

Medicine-04.question: ৩) Which one is the feature of Hypovolaemia?
৪) Glucose present in 1L 5% dextrose is?
৫) Cause of euvolaemic hyponatraemia is?
৬) Which of the following drug causes hypokalaemia?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is insulin. Insulin causes hypokalaemia by shifting potassium (K⁺) from the extracellular fluid into cells, especially skeletal muscle.

Key points:

  • Insulin stimulates Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase activity

  • ↑ Cellular uptake of K⁺

  • ↓ Serum potassium concentration

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ACE inhibitors → Cause hyperkalaemia by reducing aldosterone production.

  • Spironolactone → Potassium-sparing diuretic; causes hyperkalaemia.

  • Heparin → Can cause hyperkalaemia by reducing aldosterone synthesis (especially with prolonged use).

High-yield drug effects on potassium:

Drug Effect on K⁺
Insulin ↓ Hypokalaemia
β₂ agonists ↓ Hypokalaemia
ACE inhibitors ↑ Hyperkalaemia
Spironolactone ↑ Hyperkalaemia
Heparin ↑ Hyperkalaemia

Exam pearl:
Insulin drives potassium into cells → hypokalaemia.

Medicine-04.question: ৭) Which of the following causes normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?
৮) Diffuse soft goitre with bruit, these are typical presentation of
৯) Which of the following endocrine gland isn’t uder pituitary control?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is parathyroid glands. The parathyroid glands are not under pituitary control; they are regulated mainly by serum calcium levels through parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thyroid gland → Under pituitary control via TSH from the anterior pituitary.

  • Gonads → Controlled by pituitary gonadotropins:

    • LH

    • FSH

  • Adrenal medulla → Not controlled by pituitary; however, it is controlled directly by sympathetic nervous system.
    (Note: adrenal medulla is also not pituitary-dependent, so this question has two possible answers. In standard endocrine MCQs, parathyroid is usually the intended answer because it is a classic endocrine gland regulated by a non-pituitary feedback mechanism.)

High-yield endocrine control:

Gland Main control
Thyroid TSH (pituitary)
Adrenal cortex ACTH (pituitary)
Gonads LH/FSH (pituitary)
Parathyroid Serum calcium level
Adrenal medulla Sympathetic stimulation

Exam pearl:
Endocrine gland independent of pituitary control = Parathyroid gland.

Medicine-04.question: ১০) Which endocrine disorder causes weight gain?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is hypothyroidism. Reduced thyroid hormone levels cause a decrease in basal metabolic rate, leading to weight gain.

Features of hypothyroidism:

  • Weight gain

  • Cold intolerance

  • Fatigue

  • Constipation

  • Dry skin

  • Bradycardia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thyrotoxicosis → Causes weight loss due to increased metabolic rate.

  • Adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) → Typically causes weight loss, hypotension, and hyperpigmentation.

  • Diabetes mellitus → Classically causes weight loss (especially uncontrolled type 1 DM) due to insulin deficiency.

High-yield endocrine weight changes:

Disorder Weight effect
Hypothyroidism Weight gain
Hyperthyroidism Weight loss
Cushing syndrome Weight gain
Addison disease Weight loss

Exam pearl:
Weight gain + low metabolic rate = Hypothyroidism.

Medicine-04.question: ১১) Which of the following feature isn’t related to hypothyroidism?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is heat intolerance. Heat intolerance is a feature of hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis), not hypothyroidism.

Features of hypothyroidism:

  • Weight gain

  • Fatigue

  • Somnolence (excessive sleepiness)

  • Cold intolerance

  • Constipation

  • Dry skin

  • Bradycardia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Weight gain → Common in hypothyroidism due to reduced metabolic rate.

  • Fatigue → Common symptom of hypothyroidism.

  • Somnolence → Common due to reduced metabolic activity.

High-yield thyroid comparison:

Feature Hypothyroidism Hyperthyroidism
Weight ↑ Gain ↓ Loss
Temperature Cold intolerance Heat intolerance
Energy Fatigue, somnolence Hyperactivity, insomnia
Heart rate Bradycardia Tachycardia

Exam pearl:
Heat intolerance = Hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.

Medicine-04.question: ১২) Most common cause of hypothyroidism is?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. It is the most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas and is an autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland.

Key features:

  • Autoimmune thyroid disease

  • Anti-thyroid antibodies:

    • Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO)

    • Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies

  • May present with a firm, painless goitre initially

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Spontaneous atrophic hypothyroidism → Also autoimmune in origin but less common than Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

  • Amyloidosis → Rare cause of thyroid dysfunction due to infiltration.

  • Riedel’s thyroiditis → Rare fibrosing thyroiditis causing a hard “woody” thyroid.

High-yield causes of primary hypothyroidism:

Cause Importance
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis Most common autoimmune cause
Iodine deficiency Most common worldwide cause
Thyroid surgery/radioiodine Iatrogenic cause
Drugs (amiodarone, lithium) Drug-induced

Exam pearl:
Most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions = Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

Medicine-04.question: ১৩) Which of the following is a most common cause of hypocalcaemia?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is Vitamin D deficiency. It is one of the most common causes of true hypocalcaemia because reduced vitamin D leads to:

  • ↓ Intestinal calcium absorption

  • ↓ Serum calcium level

  • Secondary hyperparathyroidism

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Alkalosis → Causes decreased ionized calcium by increasing calcium binding to albumin, but total calcium is usually normal.

  • Hypoalbuminaemia → Causes low total serum calcium (because albumin-bound calcium decreases), but ionized calcium is usually normal.

  • Hypomagnesaemia → Can cause hypocalcaemia by reducing PTH secretion/action, but is a less common cause.

High-yield causes of hypocalcaemia:

Cause Mechanism
Vitamin D deficiency ↓ Calcium absorption from gut
Hypoparathyroidism ↓ PTH
Chronic kidney disease ↓ Vitamin D activation + phosphate retention
Hypomagnesaemia ↓ PTH secretion/action

Exam pearl:
Most common cause of true hypocalcaemia = Vitamin D deficiency.

Medicine-04.question: ১৪) Cushing’s syndrome is caused by which of the following hormone?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is glucocorticoids. Cushing’s syndrome is caused by excessive exposure to glucocorticoids, especially cortisol.

Causes:

  • Excess endogenous cortisol production:

    • Cushing disease (ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma)

    • Adrenal cortisol-producing tumour

    • Ectopic ACTH secretion

  • Excess exogenous glucocorticoid therapy

Features of Cushing’s syndrome:

  • Central obesity

  • Moon face

  • Buffalo hump

  • Purple striae

  • Hypertension

  • Hyperglycaemia

  • Muscle weakness

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Mineralocorticoids → Excess causes hyperaldosteronism (hypertension, hypokalaemia).

  • Androgens → Excess causes virilisation/hirsutism.

  • Oestrogens → Not responsible for Cushing syndrome.

High-yield adrenal hormones:

Hormone Excess causes
Glucocorticoids (cortisol) Cushing syndrome
Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) Conn syndrome
Androgens Virilisation

Exam pearl:
Cushing’s syndrome = excess cortisol (glucocorticoid).

Medicine-04.question: ১৫) Which one is not a feature of Cushing’s syndrome?
১৬) Hydrocortisone: 20 mg is equvalent to which of the following?
১৭) Features of an acute adrenal crisis excludes?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is hypertension. Acute adrenal crisis typically causes hypotension and circulatory shock due to acute deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone.

Features of acute adrenal crisis:

  • Hypotension

  • Circulatory shock

  • Hyponatraemia (due to aldosterone deficiency and cortisol deficiency)

  • Hyperkalaemia (due to reduced aldosterone effect)

  • Hypoglycaemia

  • Vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hyponatraemia → Common due to sodium loss and increased ADH secretion.

  • Circulatory shock → A life-threatening feature of adrenal crisis.

  • Hyperkalaemia → Due to reduced aldosterone causing impaired potassium excretion.

High-yield adrenal crisis:

Finding Mechanism
Hypotension ↓ Cortisol + ↓ Aldosterone
Hyponatraemia ↓ Sodium retention
Hyperkalaemia ↓ K⁺ excretion
Hypoglycaemia ↓ Cortisol

Exam pearl:
Adrenal crisis = hypotension + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia; hypertension is not a feature.

Medicine-04.question: ১৮) Acromegaly is caused by excessive secretion of which of the following hormone?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is growth hormone (GH). Acromegaly is caused by excessive secretion of growth hormone, usually from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma, after epiphyseal plate closure.

Key points:

  • ↑ Growth hormone → ↑ IGF-1 production from the liver

  • Causes enlargement of:

    • Hands and feet

    • Jaw (prognathism)

    • Facial bones

    • Soft tissues

Features:

  • Coarse facial features

  • Increased sweating

  • Headache

  • Hypertension

  • Diabetes mellitus

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Prolactin → Excess causes hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, infertility).

  • Gonadotrophins (LH/FSH) → Regulate reproductive function.

  • ACTH → Excess causes Cushing disease through increased cortisol.

High-yield pituitary hormones:

Hormone excess Condition
Growth hormone Acromegaly (adult), gigantism (child)
Prolactin Hyperprolactinaemia
ACTH Cushing disease
TSH Secondary hyperthyroidism

Exam pearl:
Acromegaly = excess GH → ↑ IGF-1 (pituitary adenoma).

Medicine-04.question: ১৯) When we comment ‘Pre-diabetes’ from plasma glucose level of a patient?
Medicine-04.option3: 2-hr glucose after 75 g oral glucose drink 7.8–11.1 mmol/L

Medicine-04.question: ২০) Anti-insulin hormone
২১) The cardinal biochemical features of diabetic ketoacidosis excludes
২২) Symptom of hypoglycaemia is..
২৩) Which drug is used as first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes in non-obese patient?
২৪) Which one is short acting insulin?
২৫) Which one is macrovascular complication DM?
২৬) During development, haematopoiesis occurs in which of the following site?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is yolk sac. During early embryonic development, haematopoiesis begins in the yolk sac around the 3rd week of gestation.

Sites of haematopoiesis during development:

Developmental stage Main site
Early embryo Yolk sac
Fetal life (main site) Liver
Later fetal life Spleen
Late fetal life → Adult Bone marrow

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Vertebrae → Bone marrow becomes an important site after birth.

  • Pelvis → Contains active red marrow in adults but not the initial embryonic site.

  • Sternum → Site of adult bone marrow haematopoiesis, not early development.

Exam pearl:
First site of haematopoiesis in embryo = Yolk sac.

Medicine-04.question: ২৭) Which is not a coagulation screening test?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is platelet count. Platelet count is not a coagulation screening test; it is a screening test for platelet number and primary haemostasis.

Common coagulation screening tests:

  • PT (Prothrombin time) → Evaluates extrinsic and common pathway (Factor VII)

  • APTT (Activated partial thromboplastin time) → Evaluates intrinsic and common pathway

  • Bleeding time (BT) → Assesses platelet function and primary haemostasis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • BT → Screening test for platelet function.

  • PT → Coagulation pathway screening test.

  • APTT → Coagulation pathway screening test.

High-yield coagulation tests:

Test Assesses
Platelet count Platelet number
BT Platelet function
PT Extrinsic pathway
APTT Intrinsic pathway

Exam pearl:
PT + APTT = coagulation screening; platelet count = platelet assessment.

Medicine-04.question: ২৮) Most common type of anaemia is
Medicine-04.option4: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is iron deficiency anaemia (IDA). It is the most common type of anaemia worldwide.

Key features of iron deficiency anaemia:

  • ↓ Iron stores

  • ↓ Haemoglobin synthesis

  • Microcytic hypochromic anaemia

  • Common causes:

    • Chronic blood loss (especially gastrointestinal)

    • Menstrual blood loss

    • Increased requirement (pregnancy, growth)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thalassaemia → Common inherited microcytic anaemia, but less common than iron deficiency anaemia globally.

  • Sideroblastic anaemia → Rare disorder due to defective haem synthesis.

  • Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia → Causes macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia, not the most common type.

High-yield anaemia classification:

Type Example
Most common anaemia worldwide Iron deficiency anaemia
Microcytic Iron deficiency, thalassaemia
Macrocytic B12/folate deficiency
Sideroblastic Defective haem synthesis

Exam pearl:
Most common anaemia = Iron deficiency anaemia.

Medicine-04.question: ২৯) Fresh frozen plasma is indicated in which of the follwoing condition?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is replacement of coagulation factor deficiency. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) contains multiple clotting factors and is used to correct coagulation factor deficiencies.

Indications of FFP:

  • Multiple coagulation factor deficiency

  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with bleeding

  • Liver disease with coagulopathy

  • Warfarin reversal (when urgent correction is needed)

  • Massive transfusion with coagulation factor depletion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Severe anaemia → Requires packed red blood cells (PRBCs).

  • Thrombocytopenia → Requires platelet transfusion.

  • Replace acute blood loss → Usually requires packed cells ± other blood components, not FFP alone.

High-yield blood components:

Component Main use
PRBC Anaemia / oxygen-carrying capacity
Platelets Thrombocytopenia
FFP Coagulation factor deficiency
Cryoprecipitate Fibrinogen deficiency

Exam pearl:
FFP = replacement of clotting factors.

Medicine-04.question: ৩০) Incase of blood group ‘O’, which antibodies present in Plasma?
৩১) Which of the following is an antiplatelet drug?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is ticagrelor. Ticagrelor is an antiplatelet drug that inhibits platelet aggregation by blocking the P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets.

Antiplatelet drugs:

  • Aspirin → COX-1 inhibitor → ↓ thromboxane A₂

  • Clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor → P2Y12 receptor inhibitors

  • Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors → abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Warfarin → Oral anticoagulant; inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X).

  • Rivaroxaban → Direct factor Xa inhibitor (anticoagulant).

  • Heparin → Anticoagulant; enhances antithrombin activity.

High-yield antithrombotic drugs:

Class Example
Antiplatelet Ticagrelor
Anticoagulant Warfarin, Heparin, Rivaroxaban
Thrombolytic Alteplase

Exam pearl:
Ticagrelor = P2Y12 inhibitor = antiplatelet drug.

Medicine-04.question: ৩২) Which of the following is the confirmatory investigation of Iron deficiency anaemia?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is serum ferritin. Serum ferritin is the most useful and confirmatory test for iron deficiency anaemia because it reflects body iron stores.

Typical findings in iron deficiency anaemia:

  • ↓ Serum ferritin (most specific indicator)

  • ↓ Serum iron

  • ↑ Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)

  • ↓ Transferrin saturation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Serum iron → Low in iron deficiency but fluctuates and is less specific.

  • TIBC → Increased in iron deficiency but not confirmatory.

  • Transferrin saturation → Reduced but less specific than ferritin.

High-yield iron studies:

Test Iron deficiency anaemia
Serum ferritin ↓ (best indicator of iron stores)
Serum iron ↓
TIBC ↑
Transferrin saturation ↓

Exam pearl:
Most specific test for iron deficiency anaemia = Low serum ferritin.

Medicine-04.question: ৩৩) Which of the following is common finding of Iron deficiency anaemia in blood film?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is microcytosis. Iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) is a microcytic hypochromic anaemia, so the peripheral blood film typically shows:

  • ↓ Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)

  • Microcytic RBCs

  • Hypochromia

  • Increased central pallor

  • Anisocytosis (variable cell size)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Macrocytosis → Seen in vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia).

  • Fragmented RBC (schistocytes) → Seen in microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (e.g., DIC, TTP).

  • Target cells → Seen in thalassaemia, liver disease, and haemoglobinopathies.

High-yield blood film:

Anaemia Blood film finding
Iron deficiency anaemia Microcytosis + hypochromia
B12/folate deficiency Macro-ovalocytes
Thalassaemia Target cells
Haemolysis/TTP Schistocytes

Exam pearl:
Iron deficiency anaemia = microcytic hypochromic picture.

Medicine-04.question: ৩৪) Which of the following is a hallmarks of haemolysis?
৩৫) Indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) (indirect Coombs test) is positive in
৩৬) Thalassaemia is a/an
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is autosomal recessive condition. Thalassaemia is inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder due to mutations affecting globin chain synthesis.

Key points:

  • Affects alpha or beta globin chain production

  • Both males and females are affected equally

  • Affected individuals usually inherit:

    • One abnormal gene from each parent

Types:

  • α-thalassaemia → Defect in α-globin gene (chromosome 16)

  • β-thalassaemia → Defect in β-globin gene (chromosome 11)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Autosomal dominant → Requires only one abnormal allele; not the pattern of thalassaemia.

  • X-linked recessive → Seen in disorders like haemophilia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

  • X-linked dominant → Affects both sexes with different inheritance patterns.

High-yield inheritance:

Disorder Inheritance
Thalassaemia Autosomal recessive
Sickle cell disease Autosomal recessive
Haemophilia A/B X-linked recessive
Huntington disease Autosomal dominant

Exam pearl:
Thalassaemia = Autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy.

Medicine-04.question: ৩৭) Which type of leukaemia is mainly found in child age group?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL). ALL is the most common type of leukaemia in children, especially between 2–5 years of age.

Key points:

  • Origin: Lymphoid precursor cells (usually B-cell lineage)

  • Common presentation:

    • Fever

    • Pallor

    • Bleeding/bruising

    • Bone pain

    • Lymphadenopathy

The other options are incorrect because:

  • AML (Acute myeloid leukaemia) → Occurs in both children and adults but is less common than ALL in children.

  • CLL (Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia) → Most common leukaemia in older adults.

  • CML (Chronic myeloid leukaemia) → Mainly affects adults; rare in children.

High-yield leukaemia age distribution:

Age group Most common leukaemia
Children ALL
Adults AML
Elderly CLL

Exam pearl:
Childhood leukaemia = ALL (most common).

Medicine-04.question: ৩৮) Which one is the most common variety of leukaemia?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). CLL is the most common type of leukaemia overall, especially in adults in Western countries.

Key points:

  • Usually affects elderly patients

  • Most common age group: >60 years

  • Characterised by accumulation of mature but dysfunctional B lymphocytes

  • Common findings:

    • Lymphocytosis

    • Lymphadenopathy

    • Recurrent infections

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ALL → Most common leukaemia in children, not overall.

  • AML → Common acute leukaemia in adults but not the most common overall.

  • CML → Less common; associated with Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL1).

High-yield leukaemia distribution:

Category Most common
Overall adult leukaemia CLL
Childhood leukaemia ALL
Acute leukaemia in adults AML

Exam pearl:
Most common leukaemia overall = CLL; most common childhood leukaemia = ALL.

Medicine-04.question: ৩৯) Most common type of hodgkin lymphoma is?
৪০) In multiple myeloma, malignant proliferation of which cell occurs?
Medicine-04.exp: Explanation:

Medicine-04.question: ৪১) Which one of the following is a causative factor for developing aplastic anaemia?
৪২) Haemophilia A occurs due to deficiency of
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is Factor VIII. Haemophilia A is caused by deficiency or dysfunction of clotting factor VIII.

Key points:

  • Inherited X-linked recessive bleeding disorder

  • Affects mainly males

  • Causes:

    • Prolonged APTT

    • Normal PT

    • Deep tissue bleeding

    • Haemarthrosis (joint bleeding)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Factor VII → Deficiency causes extrinsic pathway defect with prolonged PT.

  • Factor IX → Deficiency causes Haemophilia B (Christmas disease).

  • Factor X → Deficiency affects the common coagulation pathway.

High-yield haemophilia:

Disorder Deficient factor Inheritance
Haemophilia A Factor VIII X-linked recessive
Haemophilia B Factor IX X-linked recessive

Exam pearl:
Haemophilia A = Factor VIII deficiency; Haemophilia B = Factor IX deficiency.

Medicine-04.question: ৪৩) Conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyronine (T3) occurs in which of the following site?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is keratinocytes. Conversion of thyroxine (T4) to the more active thyroid hormone triiodothyronine (T3) occurs in keratinocytes of the skin through local deiodinase activity.

Key points:

  • Type 2 and type 3 deiodinases are involved in peripheral thyroid hormone metabolism.

  • Skin keratinocytes can convert T4 → T3 locally.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hair follicles → Involved in hair growth regulation by thyroid hormones but not the main site of T4 to T3 conversion.

  • Sebaceous glands → Not a site of thyroid hormone conversion.

  • Stratum corneum → Dead keratin layer; no active metabolic function.

High-yield thyroid hormone metabolism:

Conversion Site
T4 → T3 (activation) Peripheral tissues (liver, kidney, muscle, skin keratinocytes)
T4 → rT3 (inactivation) Peripheral tissues

Exam pearl:
Skin keratinocytes contain deiodinase enzymes responsible for local T4 → T3 conversion.

Medicine-04.question: ৪৪) Well-defined, Erythematous plaques, Silvery scale. These are typical finding of
৪৫) Tinea cruris occurs in
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is groins. Tinea cruris is a dermatophyte infection of the groin region, commonly known as jock itch.

Key features:

  • Affects groin, inner thighs, and perineal region

  • Caused mainly by Trichophyton species

  • Presents with:

    • Itchy, erythematous, annular rash

    • Raised scaly border

    • Central clearing

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Scalp → Tinea capitis

  • Nail → Tinea unguium (onychomycosis)

  • Foot → Tinea pedis (athlete’s foot)

High-yield tinea classification:

Type Site
Tinea capitis Scalp
Tinea cruris Groin
Tinea unguium Nail
Tinea pedis Foot

Exam pearl:
Cruris = crotch → groin infection.

Medicine-04.question: ৪৬) Most common organism causing Pityriasis versicolor is
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is Malassezia globosa. Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor is most commonly caused by Malassezia globosa, a lipophilic yeast that is part of normal skin flora.

Key features:

  • Organism: Malassezia globosa

  • Presents as:

    • Hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules

    • Fine scaling (“branny” scale)

    • Common on trunk, shoulders, and neck

  • More common in hot, humid climates

The other options are incorrect because:

  • M. sympodialis → Can cause pityriasis versicolor but less commonly.

  • M. furfur → Historically considered the commonest cause; now M. globosa is recognised as the predominant species.

  • Trichophyton mentagrophytes → Dermatophyte causing infections such as tinea pedis and tinea corporis, not pityriasis versicolor.

High-yield fungal infections:

Condition Organism
Pityriasis versicolor Malassezia globosa
Tinea cruris Trichophyton species
Tinea capitis Trichophyton/Microsporum

Exam pearl:
Pityriasis versicolor = Malassezia globosa (“spaghetti and meatballs” on KOH).

Medicine-04.question: ৪৭) Comedone is a Characteristic feature of
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is acne vulgaris. Comedones are the characteristic primary lesions of acne vulgaris caused by blockage of pilosebaceous follicles with sebum and keratin.

Types of comedones:

  • Open comedone (blackhead) → Oxidation of melanin/sebum at the surface

  • Closed comedone (whitehead) → Follicle remains covered

Features of acne vulgaris:

  • Comedones

  • Papules

  • Pustules

  • Nodules (in severe cases)

  • Commonly affects face, chest, and back

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Scabies → Causes intense itching, burrows, papules; not comedones.

  • Head lice → Causes pruritus and visible nits attached to hair shafts.

  • Body lice → Causes itchy papules/excoriations on clothing-contact areas.

High-yield dermatology:

Condition Characteristic feature
Acne vulgaris Comedones
Scabies Burrows + nocturnal itching
Pediculosis Nits on hair/clothing

Exam pearl:
Comedone = acne vulgaris.

Medicine-04.question: ৪৮) Histological feature of psoriasis excludes:
৪৯) Which drug causes angioedema?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is ACE inhibitors. Angioedema is a well-known adverse effect of ACE inhibitors due to accumulation of bradykinin.

Mechanism:

  • ACE normally breaks down bradykinin

  • ACE inhibition → ↑ bradykinin → increased vascular permeability → angioedema

Common features:

  • Swelling of lips, tongue, face

  • May cause life-threatening airway obstruction

  • Can occur even after prolonged ACE inhibitor use

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Gold, penicillamine → Can cause various skin reactions and hypersensitivity reactions but are not classic causes of angioedema.

  • Antimalarials → Associated with skin pigmentation, retinopathy, and hypersensitivity reactions.

  • Metformin → Commonly causes gastrointestinal side effects; angioedema is rare.

High-yield drug-induced angioedema:

Drug Mechanism
ACE inhibitors ↑ Bradykinin
NSAIDs COX inhibition → mediator imbalance
Penicillin IgE-mediated allergy

Exam pearl:
ACE inhibitor + facial/tongue swelling = bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

Medicine-04.question: ৫০) Which is not a granulocyte?
Medicine-04.exp:
The correct answer is monocyte. Monocytes are agranulocytes, meaning they do not contain prominent cytoplasmic granules.

Classification of white blood cells:

Granulocytes:

  • Neutrophils

  • Eosinophils

  • Basophils

Agranulocytes:

  • Monocytes

  • Lymphocytes

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neutrophil → Most abundant granulocyte; phagocytosis of bacteria.

  • Eosinophil → Granulocyte involved in parasitic infections and allergy.

  • Basophil → Granulocyte involved in histamine and IgE-mediated reactions.

High-yield WBC classification:

Type Cells
Granulocytes Neutrophil, Eosinophil, Basophil (NEB)
Agranulocytes Lymphocyte, Monocyte

Exam pearl:
NEB = Granulocytes; Monocyte = Agranulocyte.
